fields.Front: Name the three structural regions of the Internet and what each contains.
fields.Back:
1) Network edge: hosts (clients and servers; servers often in data centers).
2) Access networks and physical media: wired and wireless links connecting hosts to the first router.
3) Network core: mesh of interconnected routers; the 'network of networks' of ISPs.

fields.Front: What is an access network, what is the edge router, what are the three categories of access network, and what two questions should you ask about any of them?
fields.Back:
Access network: physically connects an end system to the first router (the edge router) on a path to any distant end system.
Categories: residential, institutional (school, company), mobile (WiFi, 4G/5G).
Ask: 1) bandwidth / transmission rate (bps)? 2) shared or dedicated among users?

fields.Front: Explain DSL access: infrastructure reused, devices at each end, how voice and data coexist, rates, and shared vs dedicated.
fields.Back:
Reuses the existing telephone line to the telco central office.
Home: splitter separates voice and data; DSL modem converts data to high-frequency tones. Central office: DSLAM (DSL access multiplexer) sends data to the Internet and voice to the telephone network (different frequencies on one pair).
Rates: 24-52 Mbps down, 3.5-16 Mbps up (asymmetric).
Dedicated line per home.

fields.Front: Explain cable-based access: infrastructure reused, why it is called HFC, how channels share the cable, the headend device, rates, and shared vs dedicated.
fields.Back:
Reuses the cable TV network. HFC = hybrid fiber coax: fiber from the cable headend to neighbourhood junctions, coax to homes.
FDM: video, data and control channels sit in different frequency bands of the same cable.
CMTS (cable modem termination system) at the headend (like the DSLAM); cable modem at home.
Rates: 40 Mbps-1.2 Gbps down, 30-100 Mbps up (asymmetric).
Shared: homes share the cable to the headend.

fields.Front: Compare DSL and cable access on four points: infrastructure, provider-side device, sharing, and rates.
fields.Back:
Infrastructure: DSL = telephone line to central office; cable = cable-TV network to headend (HFC).
Device: DSL = DSLAM; cable = CMTS.
Sharing: DSL = dedicated line per home; cable = shared distribution network (neighbours' downloads reduce your rate).
Rates: DSL 24-52 down / 3.5-16 up Mbps; cable 40 Mbps-1.2 Gbps down / 30-100 Mbps up. Both asymmetric.
Practical consequence: a neighbour's heavy download can slow your cable Internet (shared distribution network to the headend) but cannot slow your DSL line (dedicated pair to the central office).

fields.Front: Compare the two families of wireless access network: how end systems connect, range, rates and technology.
fields.Back:
Both are shared wireless access networks that connect end systems to a router via a base station, aka access point.
Wireless LAN (WLAN): within/around a building (~100 ft); 802.11b/g/n WiFi at 11, 54, 450 Mbps.
Wide-area cellular: provided by a mobile operator; range tens of km; tens of Mbps; 4G/5G (6G coming).

fields.Front: Classify each access technology as shared or dedicated: DSL, cable (HFC), home Ethernet, WiFi, cellular, enterprise Ethernet.
fields.Back:
Dedicated: DSL (own line to DSLAM); home Ethernet (1 Gbps per switched port); enterprise Ethernet (100 Mbps / 1 / 10 Gbps per port).
Shared: cable HFC (homes share coax to headend); WiFi (shared radio channel, 11/54/450 Mbps); cellular (shared radio, tens of Mbps).

fields.Front: Describe the host sending function in three steps and give the packet transmission delay formula it leads to.
fields.Back:
1) Take the application message.
2) Break it into smaller chunks called packets, each L bits long.
3) Transmit each packet into the access network at transmission rate R (link capacity / bandwidth, bps).
Packet transmission delay = time to push an L-bit packet onto the link: d_trans = L / R seconds (bits divided by bits/s).

fields.Front: Textbook only: how does FTTH work in a PON, and what do the ONT, splitter and OLT do? (Kurose §1.2.1)
fields.Back:
FTTH runs an optical fibre path from the central office to the home and can reach gigabits per second. Direct fibre gives one fibre per home; more commonly a fibre is shared and split close to the homes, by an active optical network (AON, essentially switched Ethernet) or a passive optical network (PON, used by Verizon FiOS).
In a PON: each home has an optical network terminator (ONT) joined by dedicated fibre to a neighbourhood splitter; the splitter combines typically fewer than 100 homes onto one shared fibre; that fibre runs to an optical line terminator (OLT) in the central office, which converts optical to electrical and reaches the Internet through a telco router.
All packets sent from the OLT are replicated at the splitter, so downstream is a shared broadcast, as at a cable headend.
Pattern: home device = DSL modem / cable modem / ONT; provider device = DSLAM / CMTS / OLT.

fields.Text: An access network connects an end system to the {{c1::edge router}}; the two things to keep in mind about it are its {{c1::bandwidth (transmission rate, bps)}} and whether access is {{c1::shared or dedicated}} among users.

DSL: {{c1::24-52 Mbps}} downstream and {{c1::3.5-16 Mbps}} upstream over a {{c1::dedicated}} telephone line to the central office, where the {{c1::DSLAM (DSL access multiplexer)}} splits data (to Internet) from voice (to phone net).

Cable (HFC = {{c1::hybrid fiber coax}}): up to {{c1::40 Mbps - 1.2 Gbps}} downstream, {{c1::30-100 Mbps}} upstream; the {{c1::CMTS (cable modem termination system)}} at the headend plays the DSLAM's role; access is {{c1::shared}} among homes.
Home network: a {{c1::cable or DSL modem}} to the headend/central office; {{c1::router, firewall, NAT}} (often one box); wired Ethernet at {{c1::1 Gbps}}; WiFi access point at {{c1::54, 450 Mbps}}.

WiFi (802.11b/g/n) WLANs reach about {{c1::100 ft}} at {{c1::11, 54, 450 Mbps}}; wide-area cellular ({{c1::4G/5G}}) reaches {{c1::tens of km}} at {{c1::tens of Mbps}}. Both connect via a base station aka {{c1::access point}}.

Enterprise access networks mix wired and wireless links connecting {{c1::switches and routers}}: Ethernet at {{c1::100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps}}, WiFi APs at {{c1::11, 54, 450 Mbps}}; an {{c1::institutional router}} provides the link to the ISP.

A sending host breaks the application message into {{c1::packets}} of {{c1::L bits}} and transmits each at the link transmission rate {{c1::R}} (aka capacity/bandwidth); the packet transmission delay is {{c1::L / R}} seconds.

Textbook only (Kurose §1.2.1): a DSL line carries three channels at different frequencies - an ordinary telephone channel at {{c1::0 to 4 kHz}}, a medium-speed upstream channel at {{c1::4 kHz to 50 kHz}}, and a high-speed downstream channel at {{c1::50 kHz to 1 MHz}}. The latest DSL standard reaches up to {{c1::1 Gbps}} downstream and {{c1::500 Mbps}} upstream, and {{c1::hundreds or thousands}} of households connect to a single DSLAM.
fields.Extra: Learn the slides' 24-52 Mbps down / 3.5-16 Mbps up for the exam; the book's figures are the modern ceiling. Actual rates are capped by tiered service pricing, distance to the CO, and wire gauge / interference.
